title: Psalm 151
lead: A short psalm in David's voice about his youth, his anointing and his victory over Goliath, printed after Psalm 150 in the Greek Psalter "outside the number." A longer Hebrew form, in two poems, was found in the Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11Q5).

sections.b: The Greek has one psalm of seven verses. The Hebrew of 11Q5 has two poems: the first (often called 151A) tells of David the shepherd-musician chosen and anointed by Samuel over his handsome brothers; the second (151B) begins "the beginning of David's mighty deeds after the prophet of God had anointed him" and breaks off as he sees a Philistine taunting Israel. Orthodox and Coptic Psalters keep the psalm; the Council of Trent counted "a hundred and fifty psalms."

sections.h: Where the Greek and the Hebrew differ
sections.b: Two lines are the ones readers look up. At 1:3 the Greek has "And who will tell my Lord? The Lord himself, he himself listens," where 11Q5 has a longer passage about who can recount the Lord's deeds, followed by "everything God saw, everything he heard, and he listened" (the transcription ends a sentence after "the Lord" and marks one letter as uncertain). At 1:4 the Greek has "his angel" where the Hebrew has "his prophet ... Samuel." Sanders, the scroll's first editor, held the Greek to be a joined and shortened form of the two Hebrew poems (Wikipedia, "Psalm 151").

sections.h: In the Psalter, outside the count
sections.b: Codex Sinaiticus's subscription counts 151 psalms; Alexandrinus counts 150 and names this psalm separately. Latin Vulgate Psalters carry it as "outside the number," and it survives in some Syriac Peshitta manuscripts. Eastern and Oriental Orthodox churches accept it as canonical; the Catholic Church considers it noncanonical (Wikipedia, "Psalm 151").
